option_description: Controls whether DNS queries leave the client encrypted via DoT (port 853), DoH (HTTPS endpoint), or DoQ (QUIC), rather than as plaintext over UDP/TCP port 53. When false, every DNS query exposes hostnames, service names, and internal topology to any passive observer on the network path.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `plaintext_dns_query_interception` whenever `not input.encrypted_dns_enabled` is true, immediately triggering a high-criticality (score 8) exposure mapped to MITRE T1040 (Network Sniffing) and T1071.004. It also gates `lack_of_mutual_authentication_between_client_and_resolver`, which fires when encrypted_dns_enabled is false and TSIG is absent. Setting this false is the single highest-impact misconfiguration in the DNS data-flow class.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check systemd-resolved for DNS-over-TLS configuration on Linux systems
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DNSOverTLS: yes and a port-853 server address confirms encrypted DNS is enabled; absence or 'no' confirms plaintext.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the systemd-resolved runtime configuration file for DNSOverTLS and DNS server settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DNSOverTLS=yes with a valid upstream resolver confirms true; missing or 'no' means false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Capture DNS traffic for 60 seconds and check whether any plaintext port-53 queries are present
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Zero packets on port 53 during normal operations strongly indicates encrypted DNS is in use; any positive count means plaintext DNS is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Kubernetes CoreDNS ConfigMap for upstream forwarding protocol
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get configmap coredns -n kube-system -o yaml | grep -A5 'forward'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A forward directive using tls:// prefix (e.g., 'forward . tls://8.8.8.8') confirms encrypted DNS; plain IP addresses indicate plaintext.

typical_values: false (default in most Linux distros and Kubernetes)
true (hardened environments using systemd-resolved DoT or enterprise DNS proxy)

option_description: Identifies the specific wire protocol used for DNS query transport: udp_plaintext (standard port 53 UDP), tcp_plaintext (standard port 53 TCP), dot (DNS-over-TLS, port 853), doh (DNS-over-HTTPS), or doq (DNS-over-QUIC). This is the most precise indicator of the actual transport in use as opposed to the boolean encrypted_dns_enabled flag.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `plaintext_dns_query_interception` independently for both `udp_plaintext` and `tcp_plaintext` values, meaning even TCP-based plaintext DNS triggers the high-criticality exposure. Only dot, doh, or doq values avoid this rule. Both plaintext enum values map to MITRE T1040 and T1071.004, representing passive interception of all DNS queries traversing the network.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use ss or netstat to identify which port and protocol the local DNS stub resolver is listening or connecting on
how_to_obtain.command: ss -tunp | grep -E ':53|:853' && resolvectl status | grep 'DNS Servers'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connections to port 853 (TCP) indicate dot; connections to port 443 indicate doh; connections to port 53 UDP indicate udp_plaintext.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform a DNS lookup and capture traffic to determine the exact transport protocol in use
how_to_obtain.command: sudo tcpdump -i any -n 'port 53 or port 853 or port 443' -c 20 & dig google.com; sleep 3; kill %1
how_to_obtain.expected_output: UDP packets on port 53 indicate udp_plaintext; TCP on port 53 is tcp_plaintext; TCP on port 853 is dot; HTTPS traffic on 443 to a DoH provider is doh.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Unbound resolver configuration for upstream protocol directives
how_to_obtain.expected_output: tls-upstream: yes with forward-addr containing @853 confirms dot; plain IP forward-addr with @53 indicates udp_plaintext.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check CoreDNS Corefile forward plugin for protocol prefix
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get configmap coredns -n kube-system -o jsonpath='{.data.Corefile}' | grep -E 'forward|tls'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'forward . tls://1.1.1.1' confirms dot; 'forward . https://...' confirms doh; bare IP addresses confirm udp_plaintext.

typical_values: udp_plaintext (overwhelming default across Linux, Windows, Kubernetes)
dot (hardened Linux via systemd-resolved or Unbound)
doh (browser-managed DoH, Pi-hole, or enterprise proxy)
tcp_plaintext (large-response fallback, some enterprise forwarders)

option_description: Controls whether the DNS resolver cryptographically validates DNSSEC signatures (RRSIG records) on every response it receives. When enabled, forged or tampered DNS responses are rejected with SERVFAIL before they reach the client, providing integrity protection independent of transport encryption.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires both `dns_response_spoofing_no_dnssec` (score 8, T1584.002) and `dns_cache_poisoning_via_birthday_attack` (score 8, T1568.003) when `not input.dnssec_validation_enabled`. Critically, cache poisoning via birthday attack fires only when BOTH source port randomization AND DNSSEC validation are absent, making DNSSEC the last-resort integrity control. Enabling DNSSEC validation alone suppresses two separate high-criticality exposures.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query systemd-resolved to confirm DNSSEC validation status
how_to_obtain.command: resolvectl status | grep DNSSEC && systemd-resolve --status | grep DNSSEC
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'DNSSEC: yes' or 'DNSSEC setting: yes' and 'DNSSEC supported: yes' confirms validation is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify DNSSEC validation operationally by querying a domain with a deliberately broken DNSSEC signature
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A SERVFAIL response (exit code 9) confirms DNSSEC validation is enforced and rejecting bad signatures; a normal response means validation is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check BIND named.conf for DNSSEC validation directive
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'dnssec-validation yes;' or 'dnssec-validation auto;' confirms enabled; 'no' or absence confirms disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test DNSSEC validation by checking for the AD (Authenticated Data) flag in a signed domain response
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The 'ad' flag present in the flags line confirms the resolver is returning DNSSEC-validated responses.

typical_values: false (default in most distributions; Ubuntu, Debian, CentOS ship with DNSSEC disabled or in opportunistic mode)
true (hardened resolvers, BIND with dnssec-validation auto, Unbound with val-permissive-mode no)

option_description: Indicates whether authoritative DNS zones hosted by this system have been signed with DNSSEC key material (DNSKEY, RRSIG, NSEC/NSEC3 records present in zone data). Zone signing is the authoritative-server complement to resolver-side DNSSEC validation; without it, downstream validating resolvers cannot verify zone integrity.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `dns_response_spoofing_no_dnssec` independently when `not input.dnssec_signing_configured`, meaning even if a resolver validates DNSSEC, an unsigned zone provides no signatures to validate and attackers can inject forged responses that pass through. This maps to MITRE T1584.002 and T1583.002 — attackers can impersonate unsigned zones without detection by any validator.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the authoritative nameserver for DNSKEY records to confirm zone signing keys are published
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more DNSKEY resource records returned confirms DNSSEC signing is configured; empty response means unsigned.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify RRSIG records are present on the SOA record, confirming the zone is actively signed
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RRSIG and NSEC/NSEC3 records alongside SOA confirms signing is active; absence of RRSIG means unsigned zone.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check BIND named.conf zone stanza for DNSSEC key file references or inline signing
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'auto-dnssec maintain;' and 'inline-signing yes;' confirms automated zone signing is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use online DNSSEC analyzer to validate signing chain from root to your zone
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Status 0 with Answer containing DNSKEY type (48) records confirms the zone is signed and reachable.

typical_values: false (majority of internal corporate zones are unsigned)
true (public-facing domains managed via Route53 with DNSSEC, Cloudflare DNS, or BIND with auto-dnssec maintain)

option_description: Defines the enforcement posture for DNS-over-TLS on port 853. 'enforced' means the client configuration actively blocks port-53 fallback and only communicates via DoT. 'opportunistic' means DoT is attempted but silently falls back to plaintext if port 853 is unreachable. 'disabled' means no DoT is attempted and all queries use plaintext.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `dns_over_tls_dot_not_enforced` (score 8, T1071.004, T1572) for both 'disabled' and 'opportunistic' values. Opportunistic mode is specifically vulnerable to downgrade attacks: an attacker blocking port 853 forces automatic fallback to plaintext port 53 with no client-visible error. Only 'enforced' mode, combined with `plaintext_dns_port_53_blocked`, prevents this downgrade. A fourth rule fires when enforcement is not 'disabled' but port 53 is not blocked, catching partial configurations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect systemd-resolved configuration for DNSOverTLS enforcement mode
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'DNSOverTLS=yes' maps to enforced; 'DNSOverTLS=opportunistic' maps to opportunistic; missing or 'no' maps to disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check if port 853 connections succeed and port 53 is simultaneously reachable to identify opportunistic mode
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 853 succeeding alone with 53 blocked indicates enforced mode; both succeeding indicates at best opportunistic; only 53 succeeding indicates disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Unbound configuration for tls-upstream and forward-addr settings to determine DoT enforcement
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'tls-upstream: yes' with no plaintext fallback addresses indicates enforced; mixed addresses indicate opportunistic.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Block port 853 temporarily and observe whether DNS resolution fails (enforced) or silently succeeds (opportunistic/disabled)
how_to_obtain.command: sudo iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 853 -j DROP && dig google.com; sudo iptables -D OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 853 -j DROP
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SERVFAIL or connection timeout confirms enforced mode; successful resolution confirms opportunistic or disabled mode.

typical_values: disabled (default on all major Linux distributions and Windows)
opportunistic (systemd-resolved with DNSOverTLS=opportunistic, common in privacy-focused configs)
enforced (hardened enterprise environments, Zero Trust network policies)

option_description: Indicates whether outbound UDP and TCP traffic to port 53 is explicitly denied at the network layer (host firewall, cloud security group, or zero-trust policy), preventing any client or application from bypassing encrypted DNS configuration and falling back to cleartext resolution.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `dns_over_tls_dot_not_enforced` when `dot_enforcement_mode != 'disabled'` but `not input.plaintext_dns_port_53_blocked`, catching a critical gap: a client configured for DoT can still be downgraded by an attacker who blocks port 853, forcing automatic port-53 fallback if the network doesn't enforce the block. This is the network-layer enforcement complement to the client-side DoT setting. Without it, DoT enforcement is advisory rather than mandatory.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check host-based iptables/nftables rules for explicit port-53 egress deny rules
how_to_obtain.command: sudo iptables -L OUTPUT -n -v | grep -E 'dpt:53|:53 ' && sudo ip6tables -L OUTPUT -n -v | grep 'dpt:53'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A DROP or REJECT rule targeting dport 53 for both UDP and TCP confirms the block is in place; absence means port 53 is open.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test whether port 53 egress is actually blocked by attempting a direct UDP DNS query bypassing the system resolver
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ';; connection timed out; no servers could be reached' confirms port 53 egress is blocked; a valid answer confirms it is open.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect AWS security group or GCP firewall rules for outbound port 53 deny rules using cloud CLI
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An empty array [] indicates no egress rule for port 53 (likely implicitly allowed); a deny rule with port 53 confirms blocking.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review nftables ruleset for port 53 drop rules on the output chain
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'drop' or 'reject' following a dport 53 match in the output chain confirms port 53 egress blocking.

typical_values: false (default; port 53 egress is open in virtually all default OS and cloud configurations)
true (Zero Trust environments, hardened Kubernetes clusters with NetworkPolicy, enterprise firewalls enforcing DNS-over-TLS)

option_description: Indicates whether a DNS-over-TLS capable upstream resolver address with explicit port 853 is configured in the local resolver or stub resolver. This is a prerequisite for DoT enforcement — even if DNSOverTLS mode is set, without a port-853-capable upstream defined, DoT connections cannot be established.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `dns_over_tls_dot_not_enforced` when `dot_enforcement_mode != 'enforced'` and `not input.dot_upstream_resolver_configured`, meaning partial DoT configurations with no actual DoT server defined are caught. This represents a misconfiguration where an operator believes DoT is in use but no valid DoT endpoint has been specified, leaving all queries traversing plaintext port 53 while the security posture assessment incorrectly assumes encryption.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check systemd-resolved configuration for DNS server entries that will be contacted over DoT
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DNS= entries such as '1.1.1.1' or '8.8.8.8' combined with DNSOverTLS=yes confirm DoT-capable upstream is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Unbound forward-zone configuration for port 853 upstream addresses
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Entries like 'forward-addr: 1.1.1.1@853' or '9.9.9.9@853' confirm DoT-capable upstream resolvers are explicitly configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify connectivity to common DoT resolver port 853 endpoints to confirm network reachability
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'CONNECTED' and 'Verify return code: 0' confirms the DoT upstream resolver is configured and reachable with valid TLS.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check CoreDNS Corefile for tls:// prefixed upstream forwarders on port 853
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o jsonpath='{.data.Corefile}' 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'tls://|:853'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'forward . tls://1.1.1.1 tls://1.0.0.1' or similar tls:// entries confirm DoT-capable upstream resolvers are configured for CoreDNS.

typical_values: false (default; most resolvers configured with plain IP upstreams on port 53)
true (systemd-resolved with Cloudflare/Google DoT, Unbound with @853 forwarders, Pi-hole with custom upstream)

option_description: Controls whether the DNS resolver uses RFC 5452-compliant randomized ephemeral source UDP ports (spanning the full 16-bit range minus reserved ports) for outgoing queries. Combined with the 16-bit transaction ID, this provides approximately 32 bits of effective entropy, making birthday-attack cache poisoning computationally infeasible without also forging the correct IP.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `dns_cache_poisoning_via_birthday_attack` (score 8, T1584.002, T1568.003) when both `not input.source_port_randomization_enabled` AND `not input.dnssec_validation_enabled`. Restricted or fixed source ports reduce entropy to as few as 16 bits (transaction ID alone), making Kaminsky-style birthday attacks feasible with tens of thousands of spoofed responses. Without DNSSEC validation as a fallback integrity control, this configuration is directly exploitable for cache poisoning and traffic redirection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test source port randomization using the DNS OARC porttest service
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A response containing 'GOOD' and a large port range spread (e.g., 'Your resolver appears to use a good range of source port') confirms randomization; 'POOR' or a narrow range indicates insufficient randomization.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Capture DNS query source ports over multiple queries and assess variation
how_to_obtain.command: for i in $(seq 1 20); do dig +short random$i.example.com @127.0.0.1 A 2>/dev/null; done & sudo tcpdump -i lo -n 'dst port 53' -c 40 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $3}' | grep -oP '\.\K[0-9]+$' | sort -u | wc -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 20+ unique source ports across 20 queries indicates strong randomization; fewer than 5 unique ports indicates poor or disabled randomization.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect BIND named.conf for port randomization configuration settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Absence of query-source with a fixed port, and a broad range in use-v4-udp-ports, confirms randomization; 'query-source port 53;' or a narrow avoid list indicates restricted ports.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Unbound outgoing-port configuration to verify a wide randomization range is permitted
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A broad outgoing-port-permit range (e.g., 1024-65535) with minimal avoid entries confirms adequate randomization; absence of outgoing-port-permit with Unbound defaults is generally acceptable as Unbound enables randomization by default.

typical_values: true (Unbound, BIND 9.7+, and systemd-resolved all enable source port randomization by default)
false (misconfigured load balancers or NAT devices that pin UDP source ports, legacy BIND configurations, some embedded DNS clients)

option_description: The effective entropy in bits used for DNS transaction ID generation. The standard 16-bit TXID field provides at most 65535 possible values; a weak or predictable PRNG reduces usable entropy below this ceiling, making IDs guessable.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires dns_cache_poisoning_via_birthday_attack when transaction_id_entropy_bits < 16 and DNSSEC validation is absent. Low entropy means an attacker can flood a resolver with forged responses across a small ID space, winning the birthday-attack race before the legitimate reply arrives and poisoning the cache.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Submit the resolver to DNS-OARC's TXID randomness test by querying the porttest.dns-oarc.net TXT record from the resolver under assessment. The response includes an entropy estimate and a pass/warn/fail rating.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A TXT record such as 'GREAT; 26 queries in 5.0 seconds from 1 ports with std dev 19869.57' — look for 'GREAT' and a high std-dev value indicating full 16-bit entropy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Capture live DNS traffic from the resolver and extract TXID values to estimate entropy empirically using tcpdump and a short Python analysis.
how_to_obtain.command: tcpdump -i any -nn 'udp port 53 and src host <resolver-ip>' -w /tmp/dns_txid.pcap -c 500 && tshark -r /tmp/dns_txid.pcap -T fields -e dns.id | sort | uniq | wc -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Unique TXID count close to 500 (near-total uniqueness) indicates high entropy; a low count relative to sample size suggests weak PRNG.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the BIND named.conf or equivalent to identify whether the resolver is compiled with or configured to use a cryptographically secure source such as /dev/urandom. Also check for any explicit random-device directive.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of 'random-device "/dev/urandom";' or no override (modern BIND defaults to secure PRNG). Absence of any override on an old BIND version is a risk indicator.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the BIND version in use; versions prior to 9.8 used a weaker PRNG. Cross-reference against known-weak versions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: BIND 9.11+ or Unbound 1.5+ indicates the resolver ships with a secure PRNG by default; older versions require explicit verification.

option_description: Controls whether the DNS server is configured to serve AXFR (full) or IXFR (incremental) zone transfer requests to secondary servers or any requesting client.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers zone_transfer_over_unencrypted_channel whenever zone_transfer_enabled is true in combination with missing TLS, missing ACL restriction, or missing TSIG. An openly accessible zone transfer hands an attacker a complete map of all internal hostnames, IP addresses, and service records without any active intrusion.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the DNS server's primary configuration file for allow-transfer, also-notify, or transfer-source directives. Any non-empty or wildcard value indicates zone transfer is enabled.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If allow-transfer is set to 'none;' or absent entirely, zone transfer is disabled. Any IP list, ACL name, or 'any;' means it is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt an AXFR zone transfer from an external or unauthorized host to confirm whether the server honours the request.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A successful response returning multiple resource records confirms zone_transfer_enabled=true. A 'Transfer failed' or REFUSED rcode confirms it is disabled or restricted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For PowerDNS, query the configuration API or pdns.conf for allow-axfr-ips or slave settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: allow-axfr-ips=0.0.0.0/0 or slave=yes without restriction confirms zone transfer is enabled broadly.

typical_values: true
false

option_description: Controls whether AXFR/IXFR zone transfer sessions are wrapped in TLS (typically DNS-over-TLS on port 853 or a dedicated TLS-wrapped TCP channel), encrypting the full zone contents in transit.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires zone_transfer_over_unencrypted_channel whenever zone_transfer_enabled is true and zone_transfer_tls_enabled is false. Without TLS, complete zone data — every hostname, IP mapping, and service record — transits the network in plaintext and is trivially captured by any passive observer on the path.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the BIND named.conf for tls stanzas associated with primaries or secondaries blocks, or listen-on directives on port 853.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of a 'tls' block referencing a key-file and cert-file, with the zone transfer channel explicitly referencing it, confirms TLS is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt a TLS handshake on port 853 of the primary DNS server to determine whether it accepts TLS connections for zone transfers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A successful TLS handshake with a valid cipher suite confirms TLS is available on the transfer channel. Connection refused or handshake failure confirms it is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Knot DNS, inspect knot.conf for tls section under the remote or acl blocks used for zone transfer peers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A tls section with cert-file and key-file populated, referenced by the remote definition, confirms zone transfer TLS is configured.

typical_values: false
true

option_description: Controls whether zone transfer requests are restricted to a defined list of authorized secondary server IP addresses or TSIG-keyed identities via an access control list, rather than being open to any requesting host.
security_impact: The Rego policy includes a condition where zone_transfer_enabled is true, transfer_acl_restricted is false, and zone_transfer_tls_enabled is false as a combined trigger for zone_transfer_over_unencrypted_channel. Without ACL restriction, any host on the network (or internet if the server is exposed) can request a full zone dump, regardless of encryption status.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the allow-transfer directive in BIND named.conf. A value of 'any' or '0.0.0.0/0' means unrestricted; a specific IP list or named ACL referencing specific IPs means restricted.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: allow-transfer { 192.168.1.2; 10.0.0.5; }; represents a restricted ACL (true). allow-transfer { any; }; or absent allow-transfer with permissive defaults is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt an AXFR from an IP address that is NOT a designated secondary server to verify the ACL is enforced.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A REFUSED response code from an unauthorized source confirms the ACL is active and restricting transfers (true). A successful transfer from an unauthorized host confirms ACL is absent or too permissive (false).

how_to_obtain.instruction: For PowerDNS, check the allow-axfr-ips configuration parameter which defines permitted transfer clients.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: allow-axfr-ips=192.168.1.0/24 indicates a restricted ACL. An empty value or 0.0.0.0/0 indicates unrestricted access.

typical_values: false
true

option_description: Controls whether Transaction Signature (TSIG) or SIG(0) keys are required to authenticate DNS messages — primarily zone transfers and dynamic updates — providing cryptographic authentication and integrity protection via HMAC shared secrets.
security_impact: The Rego policy references tsig_authentication_enabled in two rules. In zone_transfer_over_unencrypted_channel, absence of TSIG alongside enabled zone transfers and no TLS triggers the exposure. In lack_of_mutual_authentication_between_client_and_resolver, absence of both encrypted DNS and TSIG triggers the finding. TSIG prevents forged zone transfer responses and unauthenticated dynamic DNS updates even when the channel is unencrypted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search for 'key' blocks in BIND named.conf and verify they are referenced by server or zone blocks in the allow-transfer or update-policy directives.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A key block with algorithm and secret values, referenced in an allow-transfer or server block, confirms TSIG is configured and enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Knot DNS, check knot.conf for key and acl sections referencing tsig algorithm definitions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A key section with id, algorithm, and secret values confirms TSIG is defined; cross-reference with acl sections referencing the key to confirm enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt a zone transfer without a TSIG key and then with an incorrect key to verify the server requires and validates TSIG.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Both requests returning NOTAUTH or REFUSED confirms TSIG is required (true). A successful transfer without a key confirms TSIG is not enforced (false).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check systemd-resolved or stub resolver configuration on client systems for TSIG key references used in outbound queries.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of tsig-secret or key-name references in client-side resolver configuration confirms client-side TSIG authentication is configured.

typical_values: false
true

option_description: Controls whether the DNS client strictly validates the resolver's TLS certificate — including CA chain verification, hostname matching, and expiry checking — when using DNS-over-TLS or DNS-over-HTTPS, preventing connection to rogue or misconfigured resolvers.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires lack_of_mutual_authentication_between_client_and_resolver when encrypted_dns_enabled is true but resolver_certificate_validation_enforced is false and TSIG is also absent. Without certificate validation, an attacker with network position can present a self-signed or stolen certificate to intercept all DNS queries from the client, defeating the purpose of encrypted DNS.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For systemd-resolved, check /etc/systemd/resolved.conf for DNSOverTLS setting. 'yes' enforces strict validation; 'opportunistic' skips validation; 'no' disables TLS entirely.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DNSOverTLS=yes with a DNS= entry pointing to a named resolver (e.g., DNS=9.9.9.9#dns.quad9.net) confirms strict certificate validation is enforced (true). DNSOverTLS=opportunistic means validation is not enforced (false).

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Unbound acting as a local forwarding resolver with DoT, inspect unbound.conf for ssl-upstream, tls-cert-bundle, and tls-service-name directives in forward-zone blocks.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ssl-upstream: yes combined with tls-cert-bundle pointing to a valid CA bundle and tls-service-name matching the resolver's hostname confirms strict validation (true).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use openssl to test the DoT connection to the configured resolver with explicit certificate verification to confirm validation would succeed.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Verify return code: 0 (ok) confirms the certificate chain is valid and certificate validation would succeed when enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For application-level DNS clients (e.g., Python dnspython, Go net package), review application configuration or source code for TLS verification flags.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: InsecureSkipVerify: false or verify_ssl=True or cert_reqs=CERT_REQUIRED confirms validation is enforced (true). InsecureSkipVerify: true or verify_ssl=False means validation is disabled (false).

typical_values: false
true

option_description: The HMAC algorithm specified in the TSIG key definition used to compute transaction signatures on authenticated DNS messages including zone transfers and dynamic updates.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires tsig_shared_secret_replay_or_weak_mac when tsig_key_configured is true and tsig_algorithm is in ['hmac-md5', 'hmac-sha1']. HMAC-MD5 has well-known collision vulnerabilities and HMAC-SHA1 provides only 80-bit effective security; both are considered cryptographically weak for TSIG, enabling potential MAC forgery attacks against authenticated DNS transactions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect BIND named.conf key blocks for the algorithm field, which specifies the HMAC algorithm for each TSIG key definition.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A key block showing 'algorithm hmac-sha256;' or stronger is acceptable. 'algorithm hmac-md5;' or 'algorithm hmac-sha1;' indicates a weak algorithm that triggers the policy rule.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Knot DNS, inspect the key section of knot.conf for the algorithm field.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: algorithm: hmac-sha256 or hmac-sha512 is secure. algorithm: hmac-md5 or hmac-sha1 should be flagged.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use dnssec-keygen or tsig-keygen utilities to audit existing keys; their names embed the algorithm when created with standard tooling.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Key files containing 'Algorithm: hmac-sha256' or higher confirm a strong algorithm. 'Algorithm: hmac-md5' or 'Algorithm: hmac-sha1' confirms a weak configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Capture a TSIG-signed DNS transaction and decode the TSIG record to identify the algorithm name in the Other Data field.
how_to_obtain.command: tcpdump -i any -nn 'udp port 53 or tcp port 53' -w /tmp/tsig_capture.pcap -c 100 && tshark -r /tmp/tsig_capture.pcap -Y 'dns.tsig.algorithm_name' -T fields -e dns.tsig.algorithm_name
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Field value 'hmac-sha256.sig-alg.reg.int.' or 'hmac-sha512.sig-alg.reg.int.' confirms a strong algorithm. 'hmac-md5.sig-alg.reg.int.' confirms the weak HMAC-MD5 algorithm is in use.

typical_values: hmac-md5
hmac-sha256
hmac-sha512
hmac-sha384

option_description: The maximum permitted time difference in seconds between the timestamp embedded in a TSIG-signed DNS record and the receiving server's current system time, defining the window during which a captured signed message could be replayed by an attacker.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires tsig_shared_secret_replay_or_weak_mac when tsig_key_configured is true and tsig_clock_skew_seconds > 300. A large clock skew window (e.g., 3600s or 86400s) means a captured TSIG-signed zone transfer or dynamic update message remains valid for replay long after capture, allowing an attacker to re-inject previously authenticated DNS operations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the BIND named.conf for a max-skew or sig-validity-interval parameter, or look for the default 300-second value implied by absence of an override. In BIND 9.11+, the option is in the options or server block.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Absence of a max-skew directive implies the BIND default of 300 seconds. An explicit value such as 'max-skew 300;' confirms the setting; values above 300 should be flagged.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Knot DNS, inspect the server section of knot.conf for the max-timer-deviation parameter which controls TSIG clock skew tolerance.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: max-timer-deviation: 300 or lower is acceptable. Absence implies the Knot default (300s). Values above 300 indicate an overly permissive replay window.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For PowerDNS Authoritative Server, check the max-signature-validity-weeks or similar TSIG parameters in pdns.conf.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No relevant parameter found typically means the compiled default applies. Explicit overrides above 300 seconds should be documented and flagged.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Capture a TSIG-signed DNS response, delay replay by varying intervals, and observe at what offset the server starts rejecting the replayed message with BADTIME to empirically confirm the actual enforced skew window.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The fudge field value in seconds extracted from a captured TSIG record reflects the sender's declared clock skew tolerance. A value of 300 is standard; values above 300 indicate an elevated replay window.

option_description: Controls whether at least one TSIG (Transaction Signature) shared secret key is defined on the DNS server for cryptographic transaction authentication of DNS messages, particularly for zone transfers and dynamic updates.
security_impact: The Rego policy rule `tsig_shared_secret_replay_or_weak_mac` fires when `tsig_key_configured == true` combined with weak algorithms (hmac-md5, hmac-sha1) or excessive clock skew. Without TSIG configured at all, zone transfers and dynamic DNS updates carry no authentication, enabling rogue servers to impersonate legitimate peers. The `zone_transfer_over_unencrypted_channel` rule also checks `tsig_authentication_enabled` as a compensating control. Absence of TSIG means any intercepted DNS transaction can be replayed without detection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the BIND named.conf (or its includes) for 'key' block definitions indicating TSIG keys are declared.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output should show one or more 'key "<keyname>" { algorithm hmac-sha256; secret "<base64>"; };' blocks. No output indicates no TSIG keys are configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Windows DNS Server, use PowerShell to list configured TSIG resource records or check for TSIG key files in the DNS server data directory.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of .key files or TSIG RR entries confirms TSIG is configured. Empty results indicate no TSIG keys.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Unbound resolver configuration for TSIG key definitions in unbound.conf or included files.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines containing 'tsig-secret-key' or key stanza entries confirm TSIG configuration. No output indicates absence.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the DNS administrator to confirm whether TSIG keys are provisioned and ask for the key name(s) and algorithm used without revealing the secret. Request documentation of key rotation procedures.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Administrator can identify at least one named TSIG key, its associated algorithm (preferably hmac-sha256 or hmac-sha512), and the zones/servers it protects.

typical_values: false (common in small/legacy deployments)
true (enterprise environments with secondary DNS or dynamic DNS)

option_description: Controls whether DNS Response Rate Limiting (RRL) is active on the DNS server, throttling the rate at which identical or similar responses are sent to the same source, defending against both DNS amplification attacks and query flood exhaustion.
security_impact: The Rego policy rules `dns_query_amplification_and_reflection` and `dns_query_flood_no_rate_limiting` both evaluate this attribute. When `recursive_queries_publicly_accessible == true` and `dns_response_rate_limiting_enabled` is false, the amplification rule fires immediately. RRL is the primary server-side mitigation that limits the volume of spoofed-source amplification traffic a server can generate toward a victim. Without it, a 50-byte DNS ANY query can be reflected as a 3000+ byte DNSSEC response, yielding 60x amplification ratios.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check BIND named.conf options block for a 'rate-limit' stanza with defined responses-per-second threshold.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A rate-limit block with 'responses-per-second 10;' (or similar value) confirms RRL is configured. Absence of the block means RRL is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Unbound resolver, check for the 'ratelimit' directive in unbound.conf which sets the maximum number of queries per second from a netblock.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'ratelimit: 1000' or non-zero value confirms RRL is enabled. A value of 0 or absence of the directive means RRL is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Windows Server DNS, open DNS Manager (dnsmgmt.msc), right-click the server, select Properties, navigate to the Advanced tab, and look for Response Rate Limiting settings. Alternatively check Group Policy DNS settings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: DNS Manager > [ServerName] > Properties > Advanced > Response Rate Limiting
how_to_obtain.expected_output: PowerShell output shows Mode as 'Enable' with non-zero ResponsesPerSecond. GUI shows RRL enabled checkbox is checked.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform a live RRL test by sending rapid repeated identical queries from a test host and observing whether responses are truncated (TC bit set) or dropped after threshold is reached.
how_to_obtain.command: for i in $(seq 1 50); do dig +short @<dns_server_ip> ANY isc.org 2>/dev/null; done | wc -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If RRL is active, response count drops significantly after the threshold (e.g., responses-per-second 5 yields ~5 full answers then TC or NXDOMAIN slip responses). All 50 responses returning full answers indicates RRL is absent.

typical_values: false (default on most DNS servers; RRL requires explicit configuration)
true (ISP resolvers, authoritative servers handling high query volumes)

option_description: Controls whether the DNS server processes recursive resolution requests originating from arbitrary internet source IPs, effectively determining whether the server operates as an open resolver accessible to the public internet.
security_impact: This is a direct trigger in the Rego `dns_query_amplification_and_reflection` rule: when `recursive_queries_publicly_accessible == true` AND either `dns_response_rate_limiting_enabled` is false OR `dnssec_enabled == true`, the high-criticality (score 8) amplification exposure fires. Open resolvers are the primary infrastructure abused in DNS reflection DDoS attacks. DNSSEC amplifies the risk because signed responses (RRSIG, DNSKEY records) can be 10-40x larger than unsigned responses, dramatically increasing the reflective amplification ratio when combined with open recursion.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From an external IP address (outside the organization's IP space), send a recursive DNS query for an external domain to the DNS server and observe if a full recursive answer is returned.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If the server returns a full ANSWER section with A records for google.com, recursive queries are publicly accessible. A REFUSED or SERVFAIL with no answer indicates recursion is restricted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check BIND named.conf for 'allow-recursion' or 'recursion' directives that restrict which source IPs may submit recursive queries.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'allow-recursion { 10.0.0.0/8; };' restricts recursion to internal networks. 'allow-recursion { any; };' or absence of allow-recursion with 'recursion yes;' indicates open recursion.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Unbound, check access-control directives to confirm only trusted networks are permitted to submit recursive queries.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines like 'access-control: 0.0.0.0/0 refuse' followed by 'access-control: 192.168.0.0/16 allow' confirm restricted recursion. 'access-control: 0.0.0.0/0 allow' indicates open recursion.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Measurement Factory open resolver test or nmap DNS recursion script to programmatically determine if the server is an open resolver.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: nmap output showing 'dns-recursion: Recursion appears to be enabled' confirms open resolver status. 'REFUSED' result indicates recursion is restricted.

typical_values: false (correctly configured authoritative-only servers, internal resolvers with ACLs)
true (misconfigured servers, legacy deployments, small ISPs without proper ACLs)

option_description: Controls whether DNSSEC signing and validation is active on the DNS server, which cryptographically signs zone records with RRSIG/DNSKEY/DS resource records, significantly increasing response payload sizes compared to unsigned zones.
security_impact: The Rego `dns_query_amplification_and_reflection` rule fires when both `recursive_queries_publicly_accessible == true` AND `dnssec_enabled == true`, because DNSSEC-signed responses can be 10-40x larger than unsigned responses. A 50-byte query for a DNSKEY record can return a 4000+ byte signed response, creating a massive amplification factor when the server is an open resolver. While DNSSEC provides critical integrity protection (referenced separately in `dns_response_spoofing_no_dnssec`), enabling it on a publicly accessible recursive resolver without RRL and access controls substantially increases amplification risk.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the DNS server with the DNSSEC OK (DO) bit set and request DNSKEY records to determine if signed responses are returned.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response containing RRSIG and DNSKEY record types confirms DNSSEC is enabled and signing is active. Only standard SOA/NS records without RRSIG indicates DNSSEC is not enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect BIND named.conf zone declarations for 'dnssec-policy' or 'auto-dnssec' directives that enable automatic DNSSEC signing.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'dnssec-policy default;' or 'auto-dnssec maintain; inline-signing yes;' within a zone block confirms DNSSEC signing is enabled for that zone.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the DNS zone files directory for the presence of DNSSEC key files (.key and .private files) which indicate DNSSEC keys have been generated for signing.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Files named like 'Kexample.com.+013+12345.key' confirm DNSSEC keys exist. No .key files suggests DNSSEC signing has not been configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Windows Server DNS Manager or Azure DNS portal, navigate to the zone properties and check the DNSSEC signing status.
how_to_obtain.navigation: DNS Manager > Forward Lookup Zones > [ZoneName] > right-click > DNSSEC > Properties
how_to_obtain.expected_output: PowerShell shows 'IsSigned: True' and lists KSK/ZSK key details. GUI shows the zone is marked as signed with key counts displayed.

typical_values: false (majority of internal DNS zones; DNSSEC adoption remains below 30% for internal zones)
true (public-facing zones for compliant organizations, .gov TLDs, financial sector domains)

option_description: Controls whether DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) is configured and actively used by clients or resolvers in the environment, routing DNS queries over HTTPS port 443 to DoH-capable resolvers instead of standard plaintext UDP/TCP port 53.
security_impact: The Rego `dns_over_https_doh_inspection_bypass` rule fires when `doh_enabled == true` combined with either `certificate_pinning_enforced` being false or `dns_monitoring_bypass_risk == true`. DoH encrypts DNS queries within HTTPS traffic, which bypasses traditional network-level DNS monitoring (RPZ, DNS firewall, IDS DNS inspection) and can circumvent enterprise security controls. When clients use external DoH resolvers (Cloudflare 1.1.1.1, Google 8.8.8.8) without enterprise policy control, internal DNS security policies are entirely bypassed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Chrome enterprise policy configuration for SecureDnsMode and SecureDnsUri settings that control DoH behavior across managed browsers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'SecureDnsMode: secure' with a SecureDnsUri value confirms DoH is enforced via policy. 'SecureDnsMode: off' disables DoH. Absence of policy means browser default (automatic DoH upgrade) applies.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Firefox enterprise configuration for network.trr (Trusted Recursive Resolver) settings that control DoH in Firefox deployments.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'network.trr.mode: 3' means DoH-only mode is enabled. 'network.trr.mode: 0' disables DoH. Mode 2 means DoH with plaintext fallback.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check systemd-resolved or OS-level stub resolver configuration for DoH/DoT upstream settings on Linux systems.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'DNSOverTLS=yes' or 'DNSOverTLS=opportunistic' confirms DNS-over-TLS (not DoH, but similar encrypted transport) is configured. resolvectl status shows current resolver and protocol in use.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform packet capture on the network and filter for outbound HTTPS connections to known DoH resolver IP addresses to detect active DoH usage.
how_to_obtain.command: tcpdump -i any -nn 'dst host 1.1.1.1 or dst host 8.8.8.8 or dst host 9.9.9.9' and port 443 -c 100 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Captured packets to port 443 on known DoH resolver IPs (1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, 9.9.9.9, 149.112.112.112) indicate DoH traffic is flowing on the network.

typical_values: false (enterprise environments with group policy disabling DoH or enforcing internal DNS)
true (consumer endpoints, developer machines, environments using Chromium browsers with default automatic DoH upgrade)

option_description: Controls whether DoH clients enforce certificate pinning or strict CA validation constraints on their DoH resolver connections, preventing interception via rogue certificates and ensuring queries only reach approved DoH resolvers.
security_impact: The Rego `dns_over_https_doh_inspection_bypass` rule fires when `doh_enabled == true` AND `certificate_pinning_enforced` is false. Without certificate pinning or strict CA validation, an enterprise TLS inspection proxy can intercept DoH traffic with a locally trusted CA certificate, or a compromised CA can issue fraudulent certificates for legitimate DoH resolver FQDNs. This creates a scenario where DoH provides the illusion of privacy while actually exposing DNS queries to unauthorized interception. It also allows unauthorized DoH resolvers to serve responses without client detection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Chrome enterprise policy for CertificateTransparencyEnforcementDisabledForUrls and HTTP Public Key Pinning (HPKP) or pinning directives for DoH resolvers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of SecureDnsUri pointing to a specific internal DoH resolver combined with enterprise CA enrollment suggests controlled DoH. Absence of pinning configuration with external DoH resolvers indicates no pinning enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review enterprise proxy or firewall policy configuration to determine if TLS inspection is applied to port 443 traffic destined for known DoH resolver IP addresses.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules that pass or bypass inspection for DoH resolver IPs indicate no TLS interception. Rules applying ssl-bump or equivalent to those IPs indicate inspection is applied. Neither indicates no specific DoH policy exists.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Palo Alto NGFW or Zscaler Internet Access, review SSL/TLS inspection policies to confirm whether DoH resolver destinations are covered by inspection profiles and whether certificate validation is enforced.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Palo Alto: Policies > Decryption > [Policy Name] > Destination; Zscaler: Policy > SSL Inspection > Rules
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A decryption/inspection rule covering known DoH resolver hostnames or IPs with certificate validation enabled confirms enforcement. No matching rule indicates DoH bypasses inspection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the organization's PKI and certificate management policy to determine whether DoH resolver pinning is documented in security standards and whether endpoint management tools (MDM/GPO) deploy pinning configurations.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Group Policy registry values showing SecureDnsMode=2 (secure) with a specific internal SecureDnsUri indicates DoH is locked to an approved resolver with enterprise certificate trust, equivalent to pinning.

typical_values: false (most enterprise deployments lack explicit DoH certificate pinning policy)
true (high-security environments with internal DoH resolvers and MDM-enforced certificate trust)

option_description: Controls whether existing network-level DNS monitoring controls such as DNS firewalls, Response Policy Zones (RPZ), and IDS/IPS DNS inspection are effectively bypassed because DoH traffic flows over HTTPS port 443 to external resolvers outside the monitored plaintext DNS path on port 53.
security_impact: This attribute directly triggers the Rego `dns_over_https_doh_inspection_bypass` exposure when `doh_enabled == true` AND `dns_monitoring_bypass_risk == true`. When DoH traffic bypasses DNS monitoring, threat intelligence feeds applied at the DNS layer (malware domain blocking, C2 sinkholing, data exfiltration detection via DNS tunneling detection) become entirely ineffective. Attackers can use DNS-based covert channels or C2 beaconing encoded in DoH queries to exfiltrate data or receive commands while SIEM DNS log correlation produces no alerts, directly enabling T1071.004 (DNS) and T1572 (Protocol Tunneling) techniques.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Compare DNS query volumes in your DNS firewall or SIEM against expected baseline. If DoH is in use, you should see a significant drop in port 53 query counts from affected endpoints while network traffic to port 443 for DoH resolver IPs increases.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Significant drop in daily DNS query counts from specific endpoints while those endpoints remain active on the network indicates those hosts are using DoH and bypassing the monitored DNS resolver.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a monitoring vantage point, perform a packet capture on the network segment and compare DNS query telemetry (port 53) against the number of active hosts to identify endpoints generating no port 53 traffic (likely using DoH).
how_to_obtain.command: tcpdump -i eth0 -nn port 53 -w /tmp/dns_capture.pcap -G 300 -W 1; tshark -r /tmp/dns_capture.pcap -T fields -e ip.src | sort -u | wc -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Number of unique source IPs generating port 53 traffic significantly less than total active hosts count suggests some hosts are bypassing monitored DNS via DoH.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In your SIEM (Splunk, QRadar, Sentinel), run a query to identify hosts that have HTTPS connections to known DoH resolver IPs but generate zero DNS firewall log entries, indicating monitoring bypass.
how_to_obtain.command: # Splunk example: index=proxy dest_ip IN (1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, 9.9.9.9, 149.112.112.112) dest_port=443 | stats dc(src_ip) as doh_hosts | append [search index=dns_fw | stats dc(src_ip) as dns_hosts]
how_to_obtain.navigation: SIEM > Search > Custom Query for DoH resolver IPs on port 443 correlated against DNS firewall source IP coverage
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Hosts appearing in DoH connection logs but absent from DNS firewall logs confirm monitoring bypass risk is present.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the network security team to determine whether TLS inspection is deployed on the perimeter and whether DoH resolver destinations are included in inspection scope. Review firewall egress rules for port 443 restrictions to known DoH providers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Confirmation that no TLS inspection covers outbound port 443 to external DoH resolvers, combined with absence of firewall blocks on known DoH resolver IPs, confirms monitoring bypass risk is present.

typical_values: true (environments where DoH is enabled without TLS inspection or DNS resolver enforcement policy)
false (enterprises with TLS inspection proxies, internal DoH resolvers, or firewall blocks on external DoH resolver IPs)

option_description: Controls whether the recursive resolver implements RFC 7816 QNAME minimisation, sending only the minimum necessary label components of a query name to each authoritative server in the resolution chain, rather than transmitting the full FQDN to every hop.
security_impact: The Rego `information_leakage_via_query_name_minimisation_absence` rule fires when `qname_minimisation_enabled` is false AND `internal_domains_resolved == true`. Without QNAME minimisation, a query for 'secretproject.internal.corp.example.com' sends the full hostname to the root servers, TLD servers, and each delegating nameserver in the chain, leaking internal hostname structure to servers that only need to know the next delegation label. This enables passive DNS reconnaissance (T1596.001) by operators of intermediate authoritative servers and correlation attacks that map internal network topology from DNS query data.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check BIND 9.14+ configuration for the 'qname-minimization' option in the named.conf options block. BIND supports 'relaxed', 'strict', 'off' modes.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'qname-minimization relaxed;' or 'qname-minimization strict;' confirms QNAME minimisation is enabled. 'qname-minimization off;' or absence of the directive (BIND default is 'relaxed' since 9.14) indicates behavior depends on version.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Unbound resolver configuration for the 'qname-minimisation' directive and verify it is set to 'yes' in unbound.conf.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'qname-minimisation: yes' confirms the feature is enabled. 'qname-minimisation: no' or absence (Unbound default is 'yes' since 1.7.3) requires version check to determine effective setting.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check PowerDNS Recursor configuration for qname-minimization setting and verify the running version supports it.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'qname-minimization=yes' in config file or rec_control output confirms the feature. PowerDNS Recursor enables this by default since version 4.3.0.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform a DNS privacy test against the resolver using the DNS privacy test tool from Cloudflare or APNIC, or manually observe query behavior by running a test authoritative nameserver and examining what query labels arrive for a multi-level internal hostname.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A TXT response containing 'GREAT' or 'qname-minimisation: yes' from the qnamemintest.internet.nl test confirms QNAME minimisation is operational. 'qname-minimisation: no' or SERVFAIL indicates it is not enabled.

typical_values: false (BIND versions prior to 9.14, Windows DNS Server which does not support QNAME minimisation, many enterprise resolver appliances)
true (Unbound 1.7.3+ default, BIND 9.14+ default in relaxed mode, modern Linux stub resolvers with systemd-resolved 247+)

option_description: Controls whether the DNS resolver forwards or recurses queries for internal hostnames through external resolver hops, such that internal FQDNs are exposed to public resolvers or intermediate recursive infrastructure outside the organisation's control.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `information_leakage_via_query_name_minimisation_absence` when `input.internal_domains_resolved == true` and QNAME minimisation is absent. When internal zones are forwarded to external resolvers, full internal FQDNs — including sensitive service names and hostnames — are transmitted to infrastructure the organisation does not control, enabling passive collection of internal network topology via DNS/Passive DNS (T1596.001) and target reconnaissance (T1590.002).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the BIND named.conf for forward or forwarders directives on internal zones. Any zone containing 'forwarders { <external-IP>; };' or a global 'options { forwarders { ... }; };' pointing to external IPs indicates leakage.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No output or only loopback/RFC1918 IPs in forwarders blocks indicates no external forwarding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Unbound resolver configuration for forward-zone blocks that specify external name servers for internal domain suffixes.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Forward zones should reference only internal resolver IPs (RFC1918); any public IP indicates external forwarding of those zones.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform a live query for an internal-only FQDN against the configured resolver while capturing traffic on the uplink interface to observe whether the query exits the network.
how_to_obtain.command: tcpdump -i eth0 -n 'udp port 53 or tcp port 53' & dig internal.corp.example.com @127.0.0.1; sleep 3; kill %1
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Captured traffic should show DNS queries only on loopback or internal interfaces; queries appearing on the uplink confirm external recursion.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the DNS/network team to determine whether a split-DNS architecture is in place with authoritative service for all internal zones, or whether a forwarding-only resolver is used with upstream public recursors.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented confirmation that all internal zones are served authoritatively with no external forwarder for those zones.

typical_values: true
false

option_description: Indicates whether the DNS resolver or an upstream firewall enforces per-source IP query rate limits using Response Rate Limiting (RRL) or equivalent ACL-based throttling to prevent volumetric query flood attacks.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `dns_query_flood_no_rate_limiting` when `input.dns_source_rate_limiting_enabled` is false. Without per-source rate limiting, an attacker can exhaust resolver CPU, memory, or socket capacity through a flood of malformed or legitimate-looking queries (T1584.002, T1071.004), potentially causing resolver outages or triggering fallback configurations that weaken security posture.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check BIND named.conf for a rate-limit block inside the options stanza. The presence of 'responses-per-second', 'errors-per-second', or 'all-per-second' directives confirms RRL is configured.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A 'rate-limit { responses-per-second 15; };' block or equivalent confirms rate limiting is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Unbound configuration for the 'ratelimit' directive, which sets the per-IP query-per-second cap.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'ratelimit: 100' or similar non-zero value confirms rate limiting is active; absent or zero value means it is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the BIND statistics channel or use rndc to check if RRL is active and reporting drop/slip counters, confirming runtime enforcement.
how_to_obtain.command: rndc status 2>/dev/null | grep -i rate; curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8053/xml/v3/server 2>/dev/null | grep -i ratelimit
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of rate-limit counters in statistics output confirms RRL is active at runtime.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Simulate a query flood from a test source IP and observe whether the resolver begins dropping or slipping responses after the configured threshold.
how_to_obtain.command: for i in $(seq 1 200); do dig +notcp +tries=1 +time=1 nonexistent-${i}.test.example.com @<resolver-ip> &; done; wait
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If rate limiting is active, a significant portion of queries beyond the threshold will receive NXDOMAIN or no response, with counters visible in resolver logs.

typical_values: false
true

option_description: Specifies the maximum number of DNS queries per second permitted from a single source IP address. A value of 0 means no rate cap is enforced, leaving the resolver fully exposed to query flood attacks.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `dns_query_flood_no_rate_limiting` when `input.dns_source_rate_limiting_enabled == true` but `input.dns_resolver_max_queries_per_second == 0`, catching the edge case where rate limiting is nominally enabled but no effective threshold is set. An excessively high or zero limit provides no meaningful protection against volumetric floods that exhaust resolver resources (T1584.002).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract the numeric rate limit value from BIND named.conf rate-limit block. The 'responses-per-second' value represents the per-source cap.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'responses-per-second 15;' — the integer value is the effective per-source cap.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Read the Unbound 'ratelimit' value, which directly represents queries-per-second per client IP.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'ratelimit: 100' — value 0 or absence means no limit is enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows DNS Server, use PowerShell to retrieve the per-server rate limiting policy which includes the ResponsesPerSecond setting.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-DnsServerRrl | Select-Object ResponsesPerSecond, ErrorsPerSecond, WindowSize, LeakRate
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A non-zero ResponsesPerSecond value confirms a limit is set. Zero means no effective cap.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the BIND statistics HTTP endpoint for runtime rate-limit configuration values reflected in the server statistics XML.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RRL XML element containing configured limits and current slip/drop counters.

option_description: Controls whether Resource Public Key Infrastructure Route Origin Validation is enforced on BGP peering sessions that carry routes for DNS resolver infrastructure, ensuring that only cryptographically validated route announcements are accepted.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `unvalidated_routing_path_for_dns_traffic` when `input.rpki_validation_enabled` is false alongside permissive BGP filtering or absent encrypted transport. Without RPKI ROV, BGP hijacking attacks can silently redirect DNS traffic to attacker-controlled resolvers (T1583.002, T1584.002), intercepting or manipulating all resolver communications without the client detecting the routing change.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Cisco IOS-XR, display the RPKI session status and prefix validation summary to confirm ROV is configured and invalid routes are being rejected.
how_to_obtain.command: show bgp rpki summary; show bgp rpki servers
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active RPKI server sessions with 'Connected' state and a non-zero count of 'Invalid' prefixes being dropped from RIB.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On BIRD routing daemon, inspect the ROA table and routing filter policies to verify RPKI validation is active and enforced in import filters.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ROA table entries present and import filter referencing roa_check() with reject action for invalid routes.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check FRRouting (FRR) configuration for RPKI module activation and ROV enforcement policy on BGP neighbor statements.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RPKI prefix table populated with ROA entries and neighbor configurations showing 'route-origin-validation' enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the network team's BGP peering policy documentation and change records to confirm RPKI ROV is deployed in enforcing mode (invalid routes rejected) rather than merely advisory mode (invalid routes flagged but accepted).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Written policy confirming RPKI invalid prefixes are rejected on all external BGP sessions.

typical_values: false
true

option_description: Represents the level of route filtering applied to BGP announcements for paths carrying DNS resolver traffic, ranging from no filtering to full RPKI enforcement, IRR-derived prefix lists, or permissive allow-with-exceptions policies.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `unvalidated_routing_path_for_dns_traffic` when `input.bgp_route_filtering_policy` is 'none' (regardless of other controls) and also when the policy is 'permissive' or 'none' combined with absent RPKI and no encrypted transport. Weak or absent BGP route filtering enables prefix hijacking that silently redirects DNS traffic to attacker infrastructure (T1583.002, T1584.002), making the effective resolver policy irrelevant.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect BGP neighbor configurations on Cisco/FRR/BIRD for applied route-maps, prefix-lists, or filter-lists on inbound UPDATE messages. Determine if filters are IRR-derived (bgpq4 output), explicit, or absent.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each BGP neighbor toward external peers should show an inbound route-map or prefix-list. Absence of any filter on external peers indicates 'none' or 'permissive' policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for bgpq4 or IRR filter generation scripts in cron jobs or automation pipelines, which would indicate IRR-derived filtering is maintained.
how_to_obtain.command: which bgpq4 bgpq3 2>/dev/null; crontab -l 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'bgpq\|irr\|filter'; ls /etc/cron.d/ | xargs grep -l 'bgpq\|irr' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of bgpq4 binary and cron entries generating prefix-lists confirms IRR-filtered policy is actively maintained.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Cisco IOS-XR, display inbound prefix-set and route-policy assignments to external BGP neighbors to classify the filtering level.
how_to_obtain.command: show bgp neighbors | grep -E 'BGP neighbor|Route-policy|Prefix-list'; show rpl prefix-set
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each external neighbor entry should show a named route-policy or prefix-set applied inbound. Missing assignments indicate 'none'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the organisation's BGP peering policy documentation to determine the declared filtering standard (MANRS compliance, IRR filtering, RPKI-only, or open peering).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy document classifying the organisation's BGP filtering stance; cross-reference against actual router configuration for divergence.

typical_values: none
permissive
irr_filtered
rpki_enforced

option_description: Indicates whether DNS client-to-resolver communications use an encrypted and authenticated transport protocol — DNS-over-TLS (DoT, port 853), DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH, port 443), or DNS-over-QUIC (DoQ) — with certificate validation enforced to prevent interception by rogue resolvers.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `unvalidated_routing_path_for_dns_traffic` when `input.dns_traffic_uses_encrypted_transport` is false alongside absent or weak BGP route filtering. Encrypted transport is specifically cited as a mitigating control against BGP hijacking: even if routing is compromised, an attacker-controlled resolver cannot silently intercept queries without presenting a valid certificate, raising the attack cost substantially and enabling client-side detection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check stub resolver configuration on Linux clients for DoT or DoH directives in systemd-resolved or resolv.conf equivalents.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'DNSOverTLS|DNS=|DNSSEC|dns_over_tls|dns-over-https' /etc/systemd/resolved.conf /etc/systemd/resolved.conf.d/*.conf 2>/dev/null; resolvectl status 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'DNS over TLS\|Protocol'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'DNSOverTLS=yes' or 'yes (opportunistic/strict)' in resolvectl output confirms DoT is configured; 'no' means plaintext.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test whether the resolver accepts DoT connections on port 853 with certificate validation and rejects plaintext on port 53 from clients.
how_to_obtain.command: kdig -d @<resolver-ip> +tls-ca +tls-hostname=<resolver-fqdn> example.com A 2>&1 | grep -E 'TLS|Certificate|ANSWER'; nc -zv <resolver-ip> 853; nc -zv <resolver-ip> 53
how_to_obtain.expected_output: kdig showing 'TLS session' established with valid certificate and ANSWER section populated confirms DoT with cert validation. Both ports open may indicate DoT is available but not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Unbound or Knot Resolver configuration for tls-upstream, forward-tls-upstream, or equivalent directives that enable encrypted forwarding to upstream resolvers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of 'forward-tls-upstream: yes' or TLS port 853 in forward-addr entries confirms encrypted upstream transport.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Capture DNS traffic on the client or resolver interface to observe whether queries are transmitted on port 53 (plaintext) or port 853/443 (encrypted).
how_to_obtain.command: tcpdump -i any -n 'port 53 or port 853 or (tcp port 443 and host <resolver-ip>)' -c 50 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $5}' | sort | uniq -c
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Traffic appearing only on port 853 or 443 confirms encrypted transport in use; traffic on port 53 confirms plaintext.

typical_values: false
true
